  brickkit add erp/backend                    # latest tag, pinned as an exact version\n  brickkit add erp/backend@1.0.0              # a given version\n  brickkit add --local                        # every component in the local sources at once\n  brickkit add --local --init                 # ...and give each one its own local workbench first\n  brickkit add erp/backend@1.0.0 --repo       # also clone the source (at this version)\n  brickkit add erp/backend@1.0.0 --yes        # non-interactive (CI/CD)
  brickkit build                      # build every component that needs a local build\n  brickkit build erp/backend          # only this component\n  brickkit build erp/backend --force  # rebuild after changing the code
  brickkit deps\n  brickkit deps erp/backend\n  brickkit deps erp/backend@2.0.0
  brickkit fetch infra/notifier@1.0.0   fetch the artifacts of a specific version\n  brickkit fetch infra/notifier         fetch the artifacts of the latest version
  brickkit graph\n  brickkit graph > graph.mmd\n  brickkit graph --ignore-shells   ignore every shell's members and show each component as if it started on its own
  brickkit init my-project              initialize a project\n  brickkit add erp/backend@1.0.0        add a component (dependencies are pulled recursively)\n  brickkit up --dry-run                 compute without starting: see what would run and in what order\n  brickkit up                           generate deployment files and start\n  brickkit status                       show the running state\n  brickkit down                         stop (volumes are kept)
  brickkit init my-shop                 create my-shop/ with the full skeleton\n  brickkit init                         complete the current directory (asks first if it is not empty)\n  brickkit init --name my-shop --yes    complete without asking (CI)\n  brickkit init my-shop --no-skills     don't install the AI assistant skills\n  brickkit init --hooks                 only add the pre-commit hook
  brickkit lint\n  brickkit lint --strict           warnings count as failures too (CI gate)\n  brickkit lint -f deploy.prod.yaml
  brickkit local on\n  brickkit local status\n  brickkit local refresh      after the team changed deploy.yaml\n  brickkit local off
  brickkit logout\n  brickkit logout --keep-remote   delete only the local credentials, don't notify the Market
  brickkit new demo/widget                          write to components/demo/widget/\n  brickkit new demo/widget --contract openapi       also generate an OpenAPI contract placeholder file\n  brickkit new demo/widget --contract proto         also generate a proto contract placeholder file\n  brickkit new erp/shell --shell                    a shell skeleton, written to shell/erp/shell/\n  brickkit new demo/widget --path ../widget-repo    write to another directory (standalone repository case)
  brickkit publish --path ./components/people/basic\n  brickkit publish --path ./components/people/basic --visibility private\n  brickkit publish --path ./components/people/basic --changelog "added a person status field"
  brickkit release                                  the component in the current directory\n  brickkit release --path ./components/erp/backend\n  brickkit release --path svc/api                   a component in a monorepo subdirectory (tag erp-api/<version>)\n  brickkit release --local                          every local-source component of the project
  brickkit remove erp/backend                 # when it has one version\n  brickkit remove erp/backend@1.0.0           # name the version when there are several\n  brickkit remove erp/backend@1.0.0 --force   # delete the source directory even with unpushed changes
  brickkit restore           restore mode and the source layout\n  brickkit restore --check   only check whether this commit is self-consistent (a non-zero exit code means it is not)
  brickkit skills          see what is installed and whether it is out of date\n  brickkit skills update   refresh to the current CLI version
  brickkit sync   move the source of components that won't start this run into .archived/, and move back the ones that should return
  brickkit up\n  brickkit up --dry-run              only generate the files, don't start\n  brickkit up -f deploy.prod.yaml    use another deploy file (one complete file per environment)\n  brickkit up --no-local             ignore deploy.local.yaml for this run
  brickkit upgrade                    # every component with a newer version\n  brickkit upgrade erp/backend        # to the latest\n  brickkit upgrade erp/backend@2.0.0  # to a given version\n  brickkit upgrade --dry-run          # only show what would happen

BrickKit CLI working directory: caches, generated files, credentials
BrickKit CLI — build systems like snapping together bricks.\n\nYou declare which components you want and what they depend on; the CLI derives the rest and hands it to Docker, Podman or Kubernetes.\nA project is described in three layers:\n  brickkit.yaml       which components, at which exact versions\n  deploy.yaml         how they are deployed (your personal deploy.local.yaml stays out of Git)\n  config/             the environment variables each component gets\n\nWhat the CLI does:\n  1. Pull components and artifacts (Git / local directories / Market) and write them into the three layers\n  2. Resolve dependencies and work out the start order (required/optional dependencies + topological sort)\n  3. Generate deployment files, run migrations and call the underlying engine (compose / kubectl)\n  4. Build local images and release component versions (build / release / publish)\n  5. Manage the component source workspace (--repo / sync)\n\nIt is not a long-running service: it exits once the command finishes and uses no background resources.
BrickKit: the command-line tool of a declarative component assembly and management platform
Build date: %[1]s
Build the component images that need a local build
Build the images that need a local build: components without deployment.image, and components in a local install source (code under development, so the image must come from it). git and market components with an image are pulled, not built.\n\nThe image tag equals the component's metadata.version, and a shell image records the member versions compiled into it, which up checks. An existing image is skipped unless --force. The source is the local repository when it holds that version, otherwise the version's git tag is exported.\n\nup never builds: when an image is missing it fails and points here.
Building it needs its source: a git component is exported from its version tag; a market component only ships an image, so use its published image or put the source in a local install source

Create a BrickKit project, or complete one.\n\nTwo modes on the same primitive — check what a complete project has, create what is missing, leave what exists:\n  brickkit init <name>   creation: makes the directory <name>/ and the full skeleton in it\n  brickkit init          completion: fills in what the current directory lacks (an existing project,\n                         or a component repository that becomes its own local workbench)\n\nA complete project has brickkit.yaml (which components, which versions), deploy.yaml (how they are deployed),\nconfig/vars.yaml (shared values), the components/ and shell/ local sources, BRICKKIT.md (the project map) and a .gitignore.\ndeploy.local.yaml is never created here: brickkit local on makes it when you want it.\n\nIn completion mode:\n  - existing files are skipped, never touched\n  - an existing .gitignore is checked, never edited: each missing required entry is a loud warning\n    (without them personal deploy files and secrets get committed)\n  - in a non-empty directory the plan is shown first and needs a yes (--yes skips the question)\n  - the project name is --name, else the existing brickkit.yaml's project, else the directory name\n  - finally the project is loaded the way lint and up load it; if that fails, the command fails\n\nThe project name: only lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting and ending with a letter or digit\n(it names the K8s namespace and the Docker network).\n\nThe AI assistant skills (.claude/skills/, AGENTS.md) are installed too; add --no-skills if you don't want them.\nIt never touches your CLAUDE.md.\n\nWhen the project root is a Git repository root, a pre-commit hook is installed as well;\nfor a project nested inside someone else's repository, install it explicitly with brickkit init --hooks.

Download a component's artifacts (API contract, SDK, ...) without installing it into the project
Download the artifact files a component declares, but don't install it into this project.\n\nFor cross-project calls: you want the other side's .proto / openapi.json to generate a client,\nbut that service is deployed by another project, and writing it into brickkit.yaml would make the platform deploy another copy on your side.\n\nWithout a version it takes the latest version in the install source.\n\nArtifacts land in .brickkit/artifacts/<versioned-service-name>/<type>/... —\nexactly the same place as what brickkit add downloads. .brickkit/ is a local cache and is not committed to Git:\nteammates run the same fetch on their own machines; to commit the contract with the project, copy the files you need into a directory of your own.\n\nThis command is read-only: it doesn't modify brickkit.yaml, generate deployment files, or start anything.
Draw the current project's dependency topology as a Mermaid diagram and print it to stdout.\n\nWhat is in the diagram:\n  nodes     component id@version; mode: local ones are marked "managed locally" (with the port too if localPort is set)\n  solid     required dependency; dashed is an optional dependency (an optional one that can't be found is drawn as a "not installed" node)\n  greyed    components that won't start this run (turned off by mode: disable, or not running because everything above them is off)\n  shell     members hosted by a shell this run (members in the deploy file) are drawn inside their shell (subgraph)\n\ngraph never reads local mode — it reads deploy.yaml (or the file given with -f), so mode: debug, which lives only in deploy.local.yaml, never appears here.\n\nEdges are always drawn, whether or not the other end starts this run — the diagram shows the declared structure, and "started or not" is expressed by node style.\n\nNothing but Mermaid goes to stdout, so it can be saved straight to a .mmd file (brickkit graph > graph.mmd),\nand GitHub renders .mmd / .mermaid files directly; inside Markdown you must wrap it in a mermaid code fence\n(fence language mermaid) — pasting the text alone won't be rendered. Warnings from dependency resolution go to stderr.\nLike up, Market / Git components that aren't cached yet are fetched over the network for their Manifest; if the dependency graph can't be resolved it reports the same errors.

Every exposed component generates an Ingress rule for host + path: /; two identical rules pointing at different backends have no defined behavior in K8s — requests land on one of them consistently, and apply doesn't complain at all

Generate a component skeleton: a component.yaml that passes brickkit up --dry-run validation,\nand a BRICKKIT.md with the standard sections (purpose, dependencies, configuration, contracts, shell declaration)\nfor the people and AI assistants who will use the component.\n\nBy default it writes to components/<scope>/<name>/ — the local install source scans exactly this layout\n(<scope>/<name>/component.yaml), and brickkit add --repo clones source here too,\nso brickkit add --local can add it to the project with no extra configuration.\n\n--shell generates a shell (a component other components are compiled into): its component.yaml gets\nshell.members with one placeholder member to replace, and it goes to shell/<scope>/<name>/ by default\n(the local install source local-shells) — shells are project code, committed with the project.\n\n--path writes to another directory, for a component that lives in its own Git repository (one component, one repository):\nthe directory itself is then the component repository root, without the <scope>/<name> layer.\n\nIt does not run brickkit add for you afterwards: writing into brickkit.yaml is a separate, reviewable\naction. It doesn't install the AI assistant skills either — the project root already has them; in the standalone repository\ncase, run brickkit skills update yourself.

Log in to the BrickKit Market.\n\nWhat it does:\n  1. Asks for the user name in the terminal\n  2. Asks for the password in the terminal (input hidden)\n  3. Calls the Market API to verify the credentials\n  4. On success writes the token to .brickkit/credentials (permissions 0600)\n\nThe Market address is taken from the install source of type market in brickkit.yaml; if several are configured, choose with --market.\n\nToken priority: .brickkit/credentials > sources.authToken in brickkit.yaml.\nBefore each use of a token the CLI checks expiresAt; when expired it asks you to log in again (there is no automatic refresh).
Log in to the component Market; the token is stored in .brickkit/credentials
Log out of the Market: revoke the token on the server and delete the local credentials
Log out of the component Market.\n\nIt does two things:\n  1. Calls the Market's POST /auth/logout to revoke this token (the server side)\n  2. Deletes .brickkit/credentials (the local side)\n\nThe local copy is always deleted, even when the Market is unreachable — otherwise a network blip would leave someone believing they have logged out\nwhile the credentials still sit on disk. When the Market is unreachable it only warns, and says the token stays valid\nuntil it expires.\n\nWhen you aren't logged in it does nothing, and that isn't a failure.

Manage deploy.local.yaml, your personal copy of deploy.yaml
Manage local mode: your personal deploy file deploy.local.yaml (never committed).\n\nWhile local mode is on, every command reads deploy.local.yaml instead of deploy.yaml — the whole file,\nnot a merge of the two, so what you see in it is exactly what runs. That is where personal facts go:\nmode: debug for the component you are debugging, a localPort that is free on your machine, a vars value\nfor your own database, even a different target.\n\n  brickkit local on        turn local mode on; the first time, deploy.yaml is copied (only its team-file header is swapped for a personal-file one)\n  brickkit local off       turn it off (the file stays, and is used again by the next local on)\n  brickkit local status    the switch, the file, and whether the file still matches brickkit.yaml\n  brickkit local refresh   copy deploy.yaml afresh after the team changed it; the old file is kept as\n                           deploy.local.yaml.bak and every local change in it is listed, for you to merge back\n\nThe file must list exactly the components brickkit.yaml declares: when the team adds one, up refuses\nto run until you refresh (or edit the file, or turn local mode off).\nOne run can ignore the file with --no-local; -f <file> ignores it too.
Manage the AI assistant skills installed into this project (.claude/skills/, AGENTS.md).\n\nThese files are installed by brickkit init, committed with the project and shared by the team. They describe the behavior of\nthis CLI version, so they need refreshing once after a CLI upgrade.\n\n  brickkit skills          show the state of each file (read-only, same as status)\n  brickkit skills status   same as above\n  brickkit skills update   install what is missing, refresh what is outdated\n\nHand-edited files are never overwritten. update lists them and skips them. To discard local\nedits, delete that file and run update again — --force is deliberately not offered: deleting a file\nis already explicit enough, and one more switch is one more way to hurt yourself.\n\nIt also works in a standalone component repository (has component.yaml, no brickkit.yaml): there it manages only\nthe brickkit-component skill — the project-overview and assemble/deploy/troubleshoot skills make no sense there.\nThe component repository's own AGENTS.md is not touched at all.\n\nYour CLAUDE.md is not touched either: that is your own workflow file.

Move a component's default version, and the three files follow: brickkit.yaml's version and requiredBy, the deploy entries, and config/ migrated (old values copied, new keys at their defaults, dropped keys kept in the archive). When something still depends on the old version, it stays as a compatibility version. Upgrading a shell switches to the member versions the new shell compiles in.\n\nA key the user changed whose default also changed is a conflict: chosen one by one in a terminal; with --yes or without input it is written as a duplicate key, and up refuses to start until it is resolved. With no component, every component with a newer version is upgraded, all or nothing.
Move component source you don't need right now from components/ into components/.archived/.\n\nOnce a project has many components, the source you aren't touching at the moment still piles up under components/:\nIDE indexing, global search, grep, and any AI reading code for you all have to scan it too.\nsync moves it into one fixed directory — you don't have to care about it until you open it, and when you need it you know exactly where it is.\n\nThe criterion is exactly the same as brickkit up: what will start this run stays in the active directory, what won't start is archived.\nTo narrow the scope, change mode in the deploy file (turn off the top level and everything below it follows),\nand sync follows along.\n\nRules:\n\n  - Two-way: what should be archived is archived, what should be active is moved back\n  - It doesn't affect running containers and doesn't change who up will start — it only touches directories\n  - It only operates on components that are declared in brickkit.yaml and already have source\n  - The whole directory moves, .git included, so git commands keep working after archiving\n  - There is no --dry-run: if you get it wrong, run it once more and everything comes back

Publish a component to the Market (brickkit login first)
Publish a component to the Market.\n\nWhat it does:\n  1. Checks the login state (credentials or sources.authToken); errors when not logged in\n  2. Reads component.yaml in the component directory and validates the Manifest format\n  3. Checks that the image reference is valid and that every file declared under artifacts exists\n  4. Creates a draft version → uploads the artifacts → turns it stable\n  5. Sets the visibility (--visibility)\n\nPublishing in three steps is deliberate: when a version turns stable the Market checks that "the files match the artifacts declaration",\nand creating a draft first guarantees there is never a half-finished "already stable but files not all uploaded" version.\n\n--path also accepts the archive directory, for example ./components/.archived/erp/backend.

When a dependency needs another version of a component already in the project, that version is kept with requiredBy (multiple versions side by side). Adding a shell brings in the members it compiles in, at the declared versions, nested under the shell.\n\nIf the project would not load afterwards, every file is restored.

Release a component version: check, tag and push to its Git repository
Release a component without a market: a release is a Git tag, pushed to the component's own repository.\n\nThe version is metadata.version in component.yaml — the single source of truth. Only component.yaml is read;\na brickkit.yaml in the same directory (the author's local workbench) plays no part.\n\nBefore anything is written, every check must pass:\n  - component.yaml parses and validates\n  - the component directory has no uncommitted changes (for a component in a subdirectory of a monorepo,\n    only its own directory counts)\n  - the branch has an upstream and nothing unpushed: the tagged commit must already be in the remote history\n  - the tag does not exist yet, locally or on the remote\nThen the tag is created and pushed. If the push fails, the local tag is deleted again — a release either\nhappens completely or leaves no trace.\n\nThe tag is <version> when the component directory is the repository root, and <scope>-<name>/<version>\nwhen it is a subdirectory — the names the git install source reads.\n\n--local releases every component in the project's local install sources: all of them are checked first,\nthen tagged and pushed one by one. One already released (its tag is on the current commit) is skipped;\nat the first push failure it stops — earlier releases stay, later ones are not attempted.\n\nbrickkit publish (to a market) is a separate command.
Release every component in the project's local install sources

The source directory is deleted only when the last version goes, and only if nothing in it would be lost.

Restore mode in deploy.yaml and the component source layout to the last commit
Restore the mode value of each component in deploy.yaml to what the last commit has, then let the source layout follow.\n\nWho it is for: projects that removed components/ from .gitignore so component source travels with the project in version control.\nIn such projects, the directory moves made by brickkit sync land in the project's diff, and "turn off a few top-level components,\narchive with sync, forget to restore, and commit" keeps happening.\n\nIt touches only the mode field of deploy.yaml (the team file), entry by entry:\n\n  - entries present in both the working tree and the last commit → mode goes back to the committed value (the field is removed if the commit doesn't set it)\n  - entries new in the working tree (just added, or a bare id turned into id@version) → not touched at all\n  - entries in the commit but not in the working tree → never added back (this is not git revert)\n\ndeploy.local.yaml is your personal file and never committed, so there is nothing to restore it to; it is left alone.\nEvery other change is left alone too, so a component you just added is not eaten by it. Old values that get overwritten are printed before it acts.\n\n--check only checks and changes nothing: are the deploy.yaml about to be committed and the directory layout about to be committed consistent with each other?\nIf not, it exits non-zero — the pre-commit hook calls exactly this (installed by brickkit init --hooks).

Start the project in one go.\n\nHow it flows:\n  1. Load the three layers: brickkit.yaml, the deploy file (deploy.yaml; deploy.local.yaml in local mode; or the one -f names), config/, and the Manifests of all components\n  2. Decide who starts and who stops (follows the top: a top-level component without mode runs, lower ones follow the ones above)\n  3. Check required dependencies (missing → error) and optional dependencies (missing → warning, and no environment variable is injected at all)\n  4. Topological sort gives the start order\n  5. Resolve configuration, inject environment variables, merge resource quotas, and generate the deployment files:\n     compose.yaml for docker / podman, Kubernetes manifests for k8s\n  6. When there are mode: debug components, generate local-debug.<versioned-service-name>.env for you to start them from your IDE\n  7. Check images: an image built on this machine must already exist (up never builds; a missing one points you at brickkit build); a pulled image must be reachable\n  8. Call the underlying engine to start; database migrations run first (a one-shot container on Docker, a Job on K8s), and a failure blocks the main service\n  9. When there are mode: local components, up starts and supervises those host processes in the foreground; Ctrl+C stops them\n\nWhen a component's version differs from the last up, it says so, and --dry-run also prints a change summary; moving a version itself is brickkit upgrade's job.

Stop every component in one go (volumes are kept)
Stop the project.\n\nThe stop order is the reverse of the start order (dependents first, dependencies last), and is left to the engine.\n\nTo stop only a few components: write mode: disable on their entries in the deploy file, then run brickkit up.\nThe generated deployment files no longer contain them, so the engine removes the matching containers as well —\nthe effect is the same as "stop just these", and the configuration keeps a trace of it, so the next up won't bring them back.\n\nImportant: down does not delete volumes; database data is always kept.\nFor a full cleanup, run docker/podman volume rm or docker/podman compose down -v by hand.

Without network access and without needing Docker / K8s, check the YAML in this directory, read-only.\n\nTwo scenarios, decided automatically from the current directory (same rule as brickkit skills; when both are present the project wins):\n\n  Project (has brickkit.yaml)\n      Check brickkit.yaml, then the deploy files (deploy.yaml, and deploy.local.yaml when present; with -f only that file),\n      then the three layers together exactly as up loads them: every component version has one deploy entry, shell members\n      sit under a shell, $var: references are defined, config/ files match components, no duplicate keys left by an upgrade.\n      Both deploy.yaml and deploy.local.yaml (when present) must match brickkit.yaml, whether local mode is on or off.\n      Then each component's configuration against its configSchema — required items have values, written keys exist in the\n      schema, and a shell member's values can be JSON-encoded into its shell —\n      plus the shell declarations: kind: shell agrees with the shell block, and each member placed under a shell is compiled into it —\n      for every component whose manifest is on disk\n      (the .brickkit/manifests/ cache, or its local source directory); the others are listed as not checked.\n      Finally every component.yaml under the local install source (type: local) directories — whether or not it has been added.\n      The archive directory (.archived/) is not checked.\n      When brickkit.yaml itself doesn't pass, nothing after it can be trusted, so the next steps are skipped and says so.\n  Component repository (has component.yaml, no brickkit.yaml)\n      Check only that one component.yaml.\n\nIt checks the existing structural rules: required fields, types, unknown fields (spelling slips), version format, port ranges;\nthere are two kinds of warning — a misspelled key inside configSchema (such as defualt) won't take effect, and a config item name that collides\nwith a platform-reserved variable. The latter is checked more fully than up does: up only meets it when a config item has a default or is overridden by config,\nwhile lint checks every item declared in configSchema (the same scope as at Market publish time).\n\n--strict also checks references: a ${VAR} that is set neither in the process environment nor in .env, and a file:// whose file\ndoes not exist, are warnings — and with --strict warnings fail.\n\nIt does not check: whether dependencies can be resolved, or whether the member versions a shell hosts this time match the versions compiled into it — those need the resolved dependency graph, which lint deliberately never builds (that can mean a network call for a market or version-controlled component), and are left to up / graph;\nthe values behind enum, minimum and the like in configSchema (the platform doesn't validate values, see docs/en/11-reference/04-config-schema-spec.md).\n\nExit code 1 on errors; 0 with only warnings, and with --strict warnings count as failures too, for a CI gate.
